extracted.intended_audience: students learning introductory discrete mathematics / relations and functions (advanced high school or undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook guidance and exercises on relations (including equivalence relations and partitions), the integers modulo n, and functions (definitions, injective/surjective/bijective, proofs and the pigeonhole principle). Aimed at teaching rigorous definitions and proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 11.8 proved = (mod n) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; exercises ask to prove relations are equivalence relations (e.g., define R from a partition and show it satisfies these three properties). Use direct verification of each property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes and partitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalence relations partition a set; the set of equivalence classes forms a partition and conversely a partition defines an equivalence relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to list partitions for small sets and to show that the equivalence classes of = (mod n) form Z_n. The text emphasizes switching viewpoint between equivalence relations and partitions; proofs include showing P is the set of equivalence classes of R when R is defined from P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integers modulo n (Z_n) — definition of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n in N, the equivalence classes of = (mod n) are [0],[1],...,[n-1]; Z_n = {[0],[1],...,[n-1]}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate Z_5 with explicit classes and labelings; note classes can be labeled differently (e.g., [5]=[0]). Exercises ask to write addition and multiplication tables for small n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations in Z_n: definition by representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Define [a] + [b] = [a + b] and [a]·[b] = [ab] for elements of Z_n (operations defined via representatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns these definitions use representatives and raises the question of consistency. It gives a proof showing different representative choices yield the same equivalence class (well-definedness). Exercises ask to show addition is similarly consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic properties of Z_n (laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of Z_n obey commutative laws [a]+[b]=[b]+[a] and [a]·[b]=[b]·[a], and distributive law [a]·([b]+[c]) = [a]·[b] + [a]·[c].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and sample verifications are provided (including table checks). Encouraged to verify these properties directly using representative arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation from A to B (generalized relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation from set A to set B is a subset R ⊆ A×B; notation (x,y) ∈ R abbreviated xRy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show relations where domain and codomain differ (e.g., A={1,2} and B=P(A)), and diagrams illustrate arrows from elements of A to elements of B when xRy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a special relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f from A to B is a relation f ⊆ A×B such that for each a∈A the relation f contains exactly one ordered pair of the form (a,b); write f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes thinking of functions as sets (subsets of A×B) to remove ambiguity of 'rules'. Examples include numeric functions and functions between abstract finite sets; visualizations: graphs and arrow diagrams. Exercises ask to identify domain and range and list all functions between small finite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, range distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B, A is the domain, B is the codomain, and the range is {f(a): a∈A} ⊆ B. A function is surjective iff its range equals its codomain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate when range is a proper subset of the codomain (e.g., f:Z→N, f(n)=|n|+2). Emphasize checking codomain when testing equality of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f:A→B and g:C→D are equal iff A=C, B=D and f(x)=g(x) for every x in A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that identical rule/value outputs are not enough if codomains differ; functions with same domain and values but different codomains are technically not equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective, surjective, bijective (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: f:A→B is injective if for every x,y∈A, x≠y implies f(x)≠f(y). It is surjective if for every b∈B there exists a∈A with f(a)=b. Bijective if both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual descriptions and four-case diagram (injective/not, surjective/not). Exercises and examples test these definitions on common functions (e.g., polynomial, absolute value, logarithm, trig functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove a function is injective
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main approaches: direct approach (assume x≠y and deduce f(x)≠f(y)) or contrapositive (assume f(x)=f(y) and deduce x=y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrapositive is often easier when f is given by an algebraic formula because one manipulates equations rather than inequalities. To disprove injectivity, provide a counterexample: find x≠y with f(x)=f(y). Examples use contrapositive to prove injectivity for algebraically defined functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove a function is surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove surjectivity show ∀b∈B ∃a∈A such that f(a)=b (typically: suppose arbitrary b and construct or solve for an a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding an explicit preimage for an arbitrary b suffices; solving f(a)=b algebraically is common. To show not surjective, demonstrate there exists b∈B with no preimage. Examples include solving linear systems to produce preimages in Z×Z→Z×Z maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using counterexamples for non-injectivity/non-surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a function is not injective, exhibit two distinct inputs with the same output. To show not surjective, find a codomain element with no preimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several exercises prompt finding such examples (e.g., absolute-value function not injective because f(-2)=f(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole Principle (finite sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are finite sets and f:A→B is any function then: (1) if |A| > |B| then f is not injective; (2) if |A| < |B| then f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prove existence results nonconstructively (examples: equal-sum subsets among 10 integers in 1..100; two Texans with same hair count). The principle is applied by counting domain/codomain sizes and invoking non-injectivity/non-surjectivity; proofs often nonconstructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of operations defined by representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining operations on equivalence classes by choosing representatives (e.g., [a]+[b]=[a+b]), one must prove the operation is consistent (independent of representative choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text proves multiplication in Z_n is well-defined by showing if [a]=[a'] and [b]=[b'] then [ab]=[a'b']; exercise 8 asks to show addition is similarly consistent. The method: use congruence relations and divisibility properties to show representatives give same class.
